speaker: Alfred Lin
title: Benchmark Breakfast | Pat Grady & Alfred Lin on the Tactics of Great Venture Investing
question: In venture capital, why does managing senior investors primarily by outputs break down in practice?
guest: Yeah. But I think you have to realize in venture the outputs are, like, 10 years into the future. So you have outputs that look like they're outputs, but those can be mirages too, like markups can be mirages. So we don't really measure that as much as the inputs and what people do. So, like, sourcing, there's inputs, like how many quality companies have you met, or how many quality companies do you wanna bring to a Monday? And for picking, it's like the quality of your memo. Did you get to the first-order questions? Did you answer them? Did you call the right people? It's not about having a long memo, it's about getting to the right points.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Managing senior investors by outputs breaks down mainly because the outputs in venture capital arrive too late and are too noisy to manage against.

The true output, realized returns, takes roughly seven to twelve years to materialize. By the time you know whether someone was a good investor, the decisions that mattered are a decade old, and the person may have been promoted, raised a new fund, or left. Interim proxies such as markups are unreliable: they are paper valuations, often set by other investors' enthusiasm rather than company fundamentals, and can be gamed or reversed.

Returns also follow a power law, so a partner's track record hinges on one or two outliers out of a small number of deals. With samples that small, luck and skill are nearly indistinguishable, and a good process can produce bad results for years.

Attribution is murky too: sourcing, winning, board work, and follow-on decisions are often shared across the partnership, and output-based credit encourages deal hoarding and defending weak companies.

So firms end up needing to assess inputs and judgment as well: quality of reasoning, sourcing activity, founder relationships, and contribution to the partnership.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Managing senior venture investors primarily by outputs breaks down because true venture outcomes are too slow, noisy, and skewed to guide real-time accountability. Meaningful exits and realized cash distributions typically take seven to twelve years to materialize, making ultimate returns far too delayed for timely feedback, capital allocation, or course correction. Even once results arrive, venture’s extreme power-law distribution means a single outlier can mask years of flawed judgment—while macro shifts or bad luck can sink sound theses—making small-sample track records a noisy separator of repeatable skill from variance.

When firms compensate for this lag by managing to interim proxy outputs such as deal volume, capital deployed, or paper markups, they introduce severe perverse incentives. Investors are nudged to force capital out the door, chase expensive consensus rounds that reliably produce quick up-round marks, or prop up struggling portfolio companies rather than taking contrarian, asymmetric risks. Compounded by murky individual attribution across collaborative sourcing and board work, output-driven management rewards short-term gaming over the input quality—proprietary access, intellectual honesty, and founder trust—that actually drives long-term returns.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Managing senior investors by outputs breaks down mainly because the outputs arrive too late and say too little. A fund's real results, meaning realized returns and exits, take seven to twelve years to show up. By then the partner has usually raised another fund or two, made dozens more decisions, or left the firm, so the feedback is useless for managing them day to day.

The returns also follow a power law. One or two outliers drive most of a fund's results, so a small sample is mostly noise, and it's very hard to tell skill from luck, timing or market beta. A partner can make good decisions and lose, or bad ones and win. Credit is muddy too, since deals are sourced, won, approved and supported by several people.

Interim measures such as markups, TVPI and logos are easy to game and often reward momentum-chasing. As a result, firms end up judging the process instead: how well partners source deals, the quality of their theses, how rigorous their decisions are, their reputation with founders, and how much they help after investing, with outcomes treated as slow, partial confirmation.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Managing senior venture capital investors primarily by outputs breaks down because the true output of venture investing—realized cash returns—takes seven to twelve years to materialize, making it far too slow to guide ongoing management or compensation. Attempting to substitute shorter-term output proxies like markups, paper valuations, or capital deployed creates perverse incentives: they reflect broader market cycles as much as skill and reward chasing consensus, hot rounds rather than independent conviction.

Even over longer horizons, venture returns follow an extreme power law across a tiny sample size of deals per partner. Because a single outlier can dominate a career's track record, outcomes are too noisy to cleanly separate repeatable judgment from luck or timing. Finally, strict output management undermines partnership dynamics. Sourcing, winning competitive deals, and supporting founders rely on collective effort and candid debate; attributing outputs strictly to individuals discourages sharing deals, helping colleagues' portfolio companies, and voicing constructive dissent. Consequently, effective firms manage senior investors largely by observable inputs—decision rigor, sourcing quality, founder reputation, and collaboration—rather than outputs alone.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Managing senior investors primarily by outputs breaks down because the results that matter most take years to show up and are hard to attribute. A few outliers can drive fund returns, and market timing, founder execution, and colleagues’ contributions can all shape the outcome. Over any practical review period, a good investment decision can look bad, and a bad one can look good.

The outputs you can count sooner, such as deals sourced or investments closed, are easy to reward in ways that encourage activity over judgment. Passing on a weak deal, helping a colleague see a risk, or supporting a founder through a difficult stretch may create real value without producing an obvious metric.

Returns still matter over time. In the meantime, assess the quality of investors’ decisions given what they knew at the time, how they learn from misses, and what they contribute to founders and the partnership.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The output that matters most is the cash a fund returns, and that can take a decade or more to observe. Even then, a single exceptional company can drive the fund’s performance, and its success reflects the work of founders and other investors, market timing, and luck. A senior investor can make a sound decision that loses money or earn a large return for reasons they misjudged.

Shorter-term measures create a different problem. A deal-count target rewards writing a check when passing may be the better decision. Paper gains reward investments that attract a higher valuation at the next round, years before anyone realizes a return. Returns still matter, but day-to-day management also requires examining what the investor believed at the time, how they tested it, and why they invested or passed.
